Chapter 8: Inflation

Learning goals

Inflation is the growth rate of the overall price level. By the end of this chapter you will be able to:

  • measure inflation from a price index, and convert a price from one year into the dollars of another year with the consumer price index (CPI);
  • solve the quantity theory of money for the price level, \(P^* = \bar{M}\bar{V}/\bar{Y}\), and for inflation, \(\pi^* = \bar{g}_M - \bar{g}_Y\);
  • test the quantity theory with 150 years of U.S. data and with 165 economies;
  • compute real interest rates with the Fisher equation, \(i = R + \pi\);
  • explain why very high inflation is usually a fiscal problem: governments print money to pay their bills;
  • rebuild a price index from inflation rates, compute average growth rates over periods, use ratio scales with clear tick labels, and spot suspicious numbers in a data set.

# @title Helper for the website versions (run this cell; you do not need to read it)
def slider_figure(make_figure, name, values, start, label=None):
    """Precompute make_figure(name=value) for every value and join the results with one slider.

    The website cannot run Python, so each model figure gets this precomputed version.
    """
    figures = [make_figure(**{name: v}) for v in values]
    first = values.index(start)
    fig = go.Figure(layout=figures[first].layout)
    owner = []                                  # which figure each trace comes from
    for i, f in enumerate(figures):
        for trace in f.data:
            trace.visible = (i == first)
            fig.add_trace(trace)
            owner.append(i)
    steps = []
    for i, f in enumerate(figures):
        layout = {"title": f.layout.title.to_plotly_json(),
                  "annotations": [a.to_plotly_json() for a in f.layout.annotations],
                  "shapes": [s.to_plotly_json() for s in f.layout.shapes]}
        visible = [o == i for o in owner]
        steps.append(dict(method="update", label=str(values[i]), args=[{"visible": visible}, layout]))
    fig.update_layout(sliders=[dict(active=first, steps=steps, pad=dict(t=60),
                                    currentvalue=dict(prefix=(label or name) + " = "))])
    return fig

# @title Helpers for the website's country legends (run this cell; you do not need to read it)
def legend_only(fig, keep):
    """Website: every trace not named in keep starts hidden but stays in the legend (click to show it).

    Slider steps keep the choice, so a slider never switches on all countries at once.
    """
    names = [t.name for t in fig.data]
    for t in fig.data:
        if t.visible is not False and t.name not in keep:
            t.visible = "legendonly"
    for slider in fig.layout.sliders:
        steps = []
        for step in slider.steps:
            shown = []
            for name, v in zip(names, step.args[0]["visible"]):
                shown.append(v if (v is False or name in keep) else "legendonly")
            steps.append(dict(method=step.method, label=step.label, args=[{"visible": shown}, step.args[1]]))
        slider.steps = steps
    return fig


def scale_buttons(fig, ratio_ticks, start="linear"):
    """Website: linear/ratio buttons; the vertical axis then fits whatever countries are shown."""
    linear = dict(label="linear scale", method="relayout",
                  args=[{"yaxis.type": "linear", "yaxis.autorange": True, "yaxis.tickvals": None}])
    ratio = dict(label="ratio scale", method="relayout",
                 args=[{"yaxis.type": "log", "yaxis.autorange": True, "yaxis.tickvals": ratio_ticks}])
    buttons = [linear, ratio] if start == "linear" else [ratio, linear]
    fig.update_layout(updatemenus=[dict(type="buttons", direction="right", x=0.01, y=0.98, xanchor="left",
                                        yanchor="top", buttons=buttons)])
    fig.update_yaxes(autorange=True)
    return fig

Model overview

Inflation is the rate at which prices rise on average. A few percent a year hardly gets noticed, but over decades it adds up, and in some countries prices have doubled every few weeks. This chapter asks what causes inflation in the long run and what it costs. The answer it builds on is an old one: inflation happens when money grows faster than the goods and services it buys.

That idea is the quantity theory of money. Its inputs are the growth of the money supply, the growth of real GDP and the velocity of money; its outcome is the price level and the inflation rate. A second tool, the Fisher equation, links inflation to interest rates. Below we write both, define them as small functions, and add the data helpers that the sections reuse: to measure inflation in the United States and around the world, to test the quantity theory, to turn nominal interest rates into real ones, and to look at hyperinflations.

The chapter’s model is the quantity theory of money. Let \(M_t\) be the amount of money, \(V_t\) the velocity of money (how many times a year each dollar is used to buy goods), \(P_t\) the price level and \(Y_t\) real GDP. The theory has four equations (Table 8.3 of the textbook):

Equation Meaning
\(M_t V_t = P_t Y_t\) the quantity equation (8.1): money spent = nominal GDP
\(Y_t = \bar{Y}_t\) real GDP comes from the growth model (the classical dichotomy)
\(V_t = \bar{V}\) velocity is constant
\(M_t = \bar{M}_t\) the central bank chooses the money supply

Only the price level is left for the quantity equation to pin down:

\[P_t^* = \frac{\bar{M}_t \bar{V}}{\bar{Y}_t} \qquad (8.2)\]

In growth rates, the growth of a product is the sum of the growth rates, so \(\bar{g}_M + \bar{g}_V = g_P + \bar{g}_Y\) (8.3). With constant velocity, \(\bar{g}_V = 0\), and inflation \(\pi = g_P\) is

\[\pi^* = \bar{g}_M - \bar{g}_Y \qquad (8.4)\]

Inflation also links the two kinds of interest rates. The nominal rate \(i\) is paid in dollars, the real rate \(R\) in goods, and the Fisher equation says

\[i = R + \pi \qquad (8.5) \qquad\qquad R = i - \pi \qquad (8.6)\]

Python note. def creates a function: a named recipe that takes inputs (the arguments) and gives back a result with return. Writing g_V=0.0 gives an argument a default value, used whenever we do not pass one. All rates here are in percent.

def price_level(M, V, Y):
    """Equation (8.2): the price level that solves the quantity equation M V = P Y."""
    return M * V / Y


def qt_inflation(g_M, g_Y, g_V=0.0):
    """Equations (8.3)-(8.4): inflation = money growth + velocity growth - real GDP growth (percent)."""
    return g_M + g_V - g_Y


def nominal_rate(R, pi):
    """Equation (8.5), the Fisher equation: the nominal interest rate i = R + pi (percent)."""
    return R + pi


def real_rate(i, pi):
    """Equation (8.6): the real interest rate R = i - pi (percent)."""
    return i - pi

A quick check of the functions with the textbook’s examples.

Python note. An f-string such as f"V = {1000 / 200:.0f}" inserts a value into a piece of text; :.0f means “no decimals” and :.1f “one decimal”.

print(f"Nominal GDP 1,000 and money 200: velocity V = {1000 / 200:.0f}")
print(f"M = 200, V = 5, Y = 500:  price level P* = {price_level(200, 5, 500):.1f}")
print(f"Twice the money, M = 400: price level P* = {price_level(400, 5, 500):.1f}")
print(f"Money growth 7%, real GDP growth 4%:  inflation = {qt_inflation(7, 4):.0f}%")
print(f"Money growth 10%, real GDP growth 4%: inflation = {qt_inflation(10, 4):.0f}%")
print(f"Real rate 5%, inflation 3%: nominal rate i = {nominal_rate(5, 3):.0f}%")
machine_return = 5 + (100 * 1.03 - 100)         # output worth 5, plus the machine's price gain
print(f"A 100-dollar machine earns {machine_return:.0f} dollars: a nominal return of {machine_return / 100:.0%}")
Nominal GDP 1,000 and money 200: velocity V = 5
M = 200, V = 5, Y = 500:  price level P* = 2.0
Twice the money, M = 400: price level P* = 4.0
Money growth 7%, real GDP growth 4%:  inflation = 3%
Money growth 10%, real GDP growth 4%: inflation = 6%
Real rate 5%, inflation 3%: nominal rate i = 8%
A 100-dollar machine earns 8 dollars: a nominal return of 8%

Doubling the money supply doubles the price level and changes nothing real: this is the neutrality of money. And raising money growth from 7 to 10 percent raises inflation from 3 to 6 percent, one for one.

Equation (8.4) is a rule for growth rates, and it is exact only for small changes. To see how close it is, we let money and real GDP grow year by year and solve equation (8.2) in every year.

Python note. for t in range(years + 1) repeats the indented lines for t = 0, 1, …, years. rows.append([...]) adds one row to a list, and pd.DataFrame(rows, columns=[...]) turns the list into a table. .pct_change() gives the change from the previous row as a fraction.

def simulate_prices(g_M=7.0, g_Y=4.0, V=5.0, years=5):
    """Equation (8.2) year by year: money grows at g_M percent and real GDP at g_Y percent."""
    M, Y = 200.0, 500.0
    rows = []
    for t in range(years + 1):
        rows.append([t, M, Y, price_level(M, V, Y)])
        M = M * (1 + g_M / 100)
        Y = Y * (1 + g_Y / 100)
    path = pd.DataFrame(rows, columns=["year", "M", "Y", "P"])
    path["inflation"] = 100 * path.P.pct_change()
    return path


simulate_prices().round(3)
year M Y P inflation
0 0 200.000 500.000 2.000 NaN
1 1 214.000 520.000 2.058 2.885
2 2 228.980 540.800 2.117 2.885
3 3 245.009 562.432 2.178 2.885
4 4 262.159 584.929 2.241 2.885
5 5 280.510 608.326 2.306 2.885

Inflation is 2.885 percent in every year, not exactly 3: the exact rule is \(1.07/1.04 - 1\). For the rates we meet in the United States the shortcut \(\pi \approx g_M - g_Y\) is very close. For the hyperinflations of Figs. 6 and 7 it is not, but the message is the same: more money growth, more inflation.

So that a country keeps its color from chart to chart, and two countries shown together never share one, we give the colors with a small tool. Its palette has 44 colors: Plotly’s 24 dark ones, and the 20 darker ones of its 26 “Alphabet” colors.

Python note. PALETTE = [] starts an empty list, and .append adds one color at a time. In first_free, return inside a loop stops the function at the first color that fits, used.count(c) counts how often c appears in the list used, and reversed(PALETTE) walks through the palette from its last color.

LIGHT = ["#F7E1A0", "#E2E2E2", "#FBE426", "#16FF32", "#1CFFCE", "#2ED9FF"]   # too pale on white
PALETTE = []
for c in px.colors.qualitative.Dark24:                                       # 24 dark colors ...
    if c != "#2E91E5":
        PALETTE.append(c)
for c in px.colors.qualitative.Alphabet:
    if c not in LIGHT:
        PALETTE.append(c)                                                     # ... and 20 more: 44 in all
PALETTE.append("#2E91E5")                    # a medium blue, too close to the U.S. navy: used last


def first_free(used, taken):
    """The palette color least used in `used` (the group-mates' colors), preferring one no country has `taken` yet."""
    for c in PALETTE:
        if c not in used and c not in taken:
            return c
    best = PALETTE[-1]
    for c in reversed(PALETTE):                  # from the end, far from the colors always on show
        if used.count(c) < used.count(best):
            best = c                             # a big group shares out the colors evenly
    return best

Python note. group_colors walks through the countries one by one. dict(fixed or {}) starts from a copy of the fixed colors (an empty dictionary when there are none), continue skips a country that already has a color, and used collects the colors of the countries that are shown together with this one.

def group_colors(names, groups, fixed=None):
    """Give each country a color that no other country in its groups uses, as far as the palette allows.

    names: every country; groups: the lists of countries shown together (menu views); fixed: {country: color}
    for the textbook's countries, so the default view keeps the book's colors."""
    colors = dict(fixed or {})
    for name in names:
        if name in colors:
            continue
        used = []
        for group in groups:
            if name in group:
                for other in group:
                    if other in colors:
                        used.append(colors[other])
        colors[name] = first_free(used, list(colors.values()))
    return colors

Measuring inflation

We start with the facts: U.S. inflation since 1960, and the share of countries in the world with high inflation each year.

Fig. 1: The inflation rate in the United States

Goal. Follow U.S. inflation since 1960, and see how inflation rates add up to a much higher price level.

If \(P_t\) is the price level in year \(t\), the inflation rate is the percentage change \((P_{t+1} - P_t)/P_t\). Here the price level is the consumer price index (CPI), the price of a basket of consumer goods, averaged over the twelve months of each year.

Python note. pd.read_csv(...) reads a data file into a DataFrame, a table with named columns. .head() shows its first five rows.

us = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "fig8-1.csv")
us.head()
year inflation_cpi
0 1960 1.492
1 1961 1.070
2 1962 1.176
3 1963 1.256
4 1964 1.322

Inflation is the growth rate of the price level, so we can also go back from inflation to the price level. Start at 100 in 1959 and multiply by \((1 + \pi_t/100)\) year after year.

Python note. .cumprod() is the cumulative product: its first value is the first number, its second value the product of the first two numbers, and so on. .tail() shows the last five rows.

us["price_level"] = 100 * (1 + us.inflation_cpi / 100).cumprod()
us.tail()
year inflation_cpi price_level
61 2021 4.681 929.617086
62 2022 7.991 1003.902787
63 2023 4.127 1045.333855
64 2024 2.952 1076.192111
65 2025 2.634 1104.539011

They agree within 0.09 points, but the WDI stops in 2024. So we keep the textbook’s U.S. series and take every other country from the panel.

Python note. pd.concat([a, b]) stacks two tables that have the same columns. sorted(...) puts the names in alphabetical order, and .unique() lists each name once.

us_rows = us[["year", "inflation_cpi"]].rename(columns={"inflation_cpi": "inflation"})
us_rows["country"] = "United States"
all_inflation = pd.concat([panel[panel.country != "United States"], us_rows], ignore_index=True)
CHOICES = sorted(all_inflation.country.unique())
print(len(CHOICES), "economies to choose from")
200 economies to choose from

The chart has two views. The price level is shown on a ratio scale, where equal distances mean equal percentage changes, so a steeper line means faster inflation. Each country’s price level starts at 100 in the year before its first inflation rate (1959 for the United States). Inflation rates differ hugely across countries, so the top of the inflation axis moves up in steps (15, 30, 60, 120, 250, 500 percent) when a country needs it.

Python note. if ... else runs one block of code or the other, and return inside a loop stops the function at the first match. With log_y=True the vertical axis is a ratio scale; tickvals chooses the numbers printed on it, and the range of a ratio axis is given in powers of 10 (np.log10(80)).

PRICE_TICKS = [100, 200, 400, 800, 1600]
CAPS = [15, 30, 60, 120, 250, 500]               # possible tops of the inflation axis


def axis_top(value, caps):
    """The smallest number in caps that is at least value (the largest one if none is)."""
    for cap in caps:
        if value <= cap:
            return cap
    return caps[-1]


def price_index(rates):
    """Fig. 8.1: the price level implied by inflation rates (100 in the year before the first rate)."""
    return 100 * (1 + rates / 100).cumprod()

Python note. px.line(..., color="country") draws one line per country, and color_discrete_map=INFLATION_COLORS fixes each country’s color. data.loc[data.inflation.idxmax()] is the row with the highest inflation.

def rate_view(data):
    """Fig. 8.1, inflation rates: one line per country; the top of the axis rises in steps."""
    top = axis_top(data.inflation.max(), CAPS)
    fig = px.line(data, x="year", y="inflation", color="country", hover_name="country",
                  color_discrete_map=INFLATION_COLORS,
                  labels={"year": "Year", "inflation": "Inflation rate (percent)", "country": "Country"})
    fig.update_traces(line=dict(width=2))
    if data.country.nunique() == 1:
        fig.update_traces(fill="tozeroy")               # one country: an area chart, as in the textbook
    fig.add_hline(y=0, line_dash="dash", line_color=GRAY)
    fig.update_yaxes(range=[-2 * top / 15, top])
    peak = data.loc[data.inflation.idxmax()]
    title = f"{peak.country}: inflation peaked at {peak.inflation:,.1f}% in {peak.year:.0f}"
    if peak.inflation > top:
        title = f"{peak.country}: inflation peaked at {peak.inflation:,.0f}% in {peak.year:.0f} (axis cut at {top}%)"
    elif data.country.nunique() == 1:
        title = title + f"; {data.year.iloc[-1]}: {data.inflation.iloc[-1]:.1f}%"
    return fig, title
def level_view(data):
    """Fig. 8.1, price levels on a ratio scale (100 in the year before each country's first rate)."""
    fig = px.line(data, x="year", y="price_level", color="country", log_y=True, hover_name="country",
                  color_discrete_map=INFLATION_COLORS,
                  labels={"year": "Year", "price_level": "Price level (start = 100, ratio scale)", "country": "Country"})
    fig.update_traces(line=dict(width=3))
    top = data.price_level.max()
    if top < 1500:
        fig.update_yaxes(tickvals=PRICE_TICKS, range=[np.log10(80), np.log10(1500)])
    else:
        fig.update_yaxes(dtick=1, exponentformat="power", range=[np.log10(80), np.log10(2 * top)])   # ticks 10², 10³, ...
    peak = data.loc[data.price_level.idxmax()]
    start = data[data.country == peak.country].year.min() - 1
    factor = f"{peak.price_level / 100:,.3g}" if peak.price_level < 1e8 else f"about 10^{np.log10(peak.price_level / 100):.0f}"
    return fig, f"{peak.country}: prices rose {factor}-fold from {start} to {peak.year:.0f}"

Python note. groupby("country").inflation.transform(price_index) runs price_index separately on each country’s rates and puts the results back in the original rows. .copy() makes a separate table, so that adding a column does not touch all_inflation.

def inflation_chart(view="inflation rate", countries=("United States",)):
    """Fig. 8.1: CPI inflation, or the price level it adds up to, for the chosen countries."""
    if len(countries) == 0:
        countries = ("United States",)                 # nothing chosen: show the textbook's country
    data = all_inflation[all_inflation.country.isin(countries)].sort_values(["country", "year"]).copy()
    if view == "inflation rate":
        fig, title = rate_view(data)
    else:
        data["price_level"] = data.groupby("country").inflation.transform(price_index)
        fig, title = level_view(data)
    fig.update_layout(title=title, legend_title_text="")
    return fig

Python note. interact calls the function and redraws its figure every time you change a widget. ToggleButtons shows one button per option, and the function receives the text of the chosen button. SelectMultiple is a list from which you can pick several countries: hold Ctrl (Cmd on a Mac) and click. The function receives the chosen names as a tuple, a list that cannot be changed. The ; at the end only hides an extra line of text.

interact(inflation_chart, view=ToggleButtons(options=["inflation rate", "price level"], description="show"),
         countries=SelectMultiple(options=CHOICES, value=["United States"], rows=8, description="countries"));

Sources. Data: U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, Consumer Price Index for All Urban Consumers (CPIAUCSL), via FRED, annual averages, for the United States; World Bank, World Development Indicators, Inflation, consumer prices (FP.CPI.TOTL.ZG) for the other economies, with gaps filled from the World Bank’s Global Inflation Database (Ha, Kose and Ohnsorge 2023). Prepared files: data/ch08/fig8-1.csv, data/ch08/inflation_panel.csv and data/ch08/countries.csv (see the data notes). Chart: inspired by Fig. 8.1 in Jones (2024), Macroeconomics, 6th ed.

On the website, click a country in the legend to add it (the G20 economies are listed; in Colab you can choose any of the 200).

What to notice.

  • Inflation was low in the early 1960s, rose through the late 1960s and 1970s (the “Great Inflation”), and peaked at 13.5 percent in 1980.
  • It fell sharply in the early 1980s, and from 1992 to 2020 it stayed below 4 percent. The Covid-19 years brought it back to 8.0 percent in 2022.
  • In 2009 the rate was slightly negative: prices fell. That is deflation.
  • Switch to the price level: prices are about 11 times their 1959 level. The line never falls for long, and it is steepest in the 1970s.
  • Add Germany and Japan. The Great Inflation was a rich-world event, but its size differed: Germany peaked at only 7.0 percent in 1973, Japan at 23.2 percent in 1974. In the price-level view, Japan’s line is almost flat from the mid-1990s to 2021: prices fell in 15 of those 27 years.

Key numbers: the Great Inflation and after

Python note. set_index("year") uses the years as row labels, so rate.loc[1960:1964] keeps the rows from 1960 to 1964 and rate[1980] picks one number.

print(f"Average 2000-2019:  {rate.loc[2000:2019].mean():.2f}%")
print(f"2009: {rate[2009]:.2f}%   2022: {rate[2022]:.2f}%   {rate.index[-1]}: {rate.iloc[-1]:.2f}%")

Peak:               13.50% in 1980
Average 2000-2019:  2.17%
2009: -0.32%   2022: 7.99%   2025: 2.63%

The textbook’s numbers hold: about 1.3 percent a year in the early 1960s (“on the order of 2 percent”), a peak of 13.50 percent in 1980, about 2 percent in 2000–2019, and 7.99 percent in 2022. By 2025 inflation was down to 2.63 percent.

Every cell of the textbook’s table is reproduced. To move a price from one year to another, multiply by the ratio of the two price levels: \(0.27 \times 100/8.23\) for 1950 to 2022.

def in_dollars_of(price, year, to_year=2025):
    """Table 8.1 case study: the value of `price` dollars of `year`, in dollars of `to_year`."""
    return price * cpi[to_year] / cpi[year]


print(f"27 cents of 1950 = {in_dollars_of(0.27, 1950, 2022):.2f} dollars of 2022 = {in_dollars_of(0.27, 1950):.2f} dollars of 2025")
print(f"Prices rose {100 * (cpi[2025] / cpi[2022] - 1):.1f}% from 2022 to 2025")
print(f"A 10,000-dollar pension of 1970 bought in 1983 what {in_dollars_of(10000, 1983, 1970):,.0f} dollars bought in 1970")
27 cents of 1950 = 3.28 dollars of 2022 = 3.61 dollars of 2025
Prices rose 10.0% from 2022 to 2025
A 10,000-dollar pension of 1970 bought in 1983 what 3,900 dollars bought in 1970

Gasoline at 27 cents in 1950 cost $3.28 in 2022 dollars, just a little less than its 2022 price. The last line is Mr. Gambino from the textbook’s Section 8.4: a fixed pension of $10,000 set in 1970 had lost 61 percent of its value by 1983, and was worth about $3,900 of 1970 dollars (the textbook says 40 percent, $4,000).

Goal. See that high inflation was common around the world in the 1970s–1990s, and rare since 2000.

For each year, the textbook counts the share of countries with inflation above 25 percent. The file has this share, and the number of countries with data in each year.

To try other thresholds we need the inflation rate of every country in every year: the panel of Fig. 1. To redraw Fig. 8.2 we keep only its WDI rows, the data behind the textbook’s figure.

Python note. panel[panel.source == "WDI"] keeps the rows where the condition is true. wdi.inflation > threshold is a column of True/False values; its .mean() is the share of True values, because True counts as 1 and False as 0. groupby(wdi.year) computes this share separately for each year.

wdi = panel[panel.source == "WDI"]
share_25 = 100 * (wdi.inflation > 25).groupby(wdi.year).mean()
print(f"Largest difference from fig8-2.csv: {(share_25.values - high.share_above_25_pct.values).max():.3f} points")
Largest difference from fig8-2.csv: 0.000 points

The threshold of 25 percent reproduces the file of Fig. 8.2. Was high inflation a worldwide event, or did it hit some regions more than others? With the region of every economy from countries.csv we can compute the same share for a group of economies: the World Bank’s seven regions, or the OECD members.

Python note. .isin(codes) is True for the rows whose code is in codes. .size() counts the rows of each group: here, the number of economies with data in each year.

GROUPS = ["World", "OECD members"] + sorted(countries.region.unique())
GROUP_COLORS = group_colors(GROUPS, [GROUPS], {"World": BLUE})   # the World keeps the textbook's blue


def group_share(threshold, group):
    """Fig. 8.2: the percentage of a group's reporting economies with inflation above `threshold`, by year."""
    if group == "World":
        members = countries.iso3
    elif group == "OECD members":
        members = countries.iso3[countries.oecd]
    else:
        members = countries.iso3[countries.region == group]
    sub = wdi[wdi.iso3.isin(members)]
    share = (100 * (sub.inflation > threshold).groupby(sub.year).mean()).reset_index(name="share")
    share["economies"] = sub.groupby("year").size().values
    share["group"] = group
    return share
def high_inflation_share(threshold=25, groups=("World",)):
    """Fig. 8.2: the percentage of economies with inflation above `threshold` percent, for each group."""
    if len(groups) == 0:
        groups = ("World",)                             # nothing chosen: the textbook's view
    tables = []
    for group in groups:
        tables.append(group_share(threshold, group))
    shares = pd.concat(tables)
    first = shares[shares.group == groups[0]]
    peak = first.loc[first.share.idxmax()]
    fig = px.line(shares, x="year", y="share", color="group", hover_name="group", hover_data=["economies"],
                  color_discrete_map=GROUP_COLORS, labels={"year": "Year", "share": "Fraction of countries (percent)"},
                  title=f"Inflation above {threshold}%: {groups[0]} peaked at {peak.share:.1f}% in {peak.year:.0f}")
    fig.update_traces(line=dict(width=2))
    if len(groups) == 1:
        fig.update_traces(fill="tozeroy")               # one group: an area chart, as in the textbook
    fig.update_yaxes(range=[0, 104], tickvals=[20, 40, 60, 80, 100])   # no label in the bottom-left corner
    fig.update_layout(legend_title_text="")
    return fig

Python note. A Dropdown is a menu: the function receives the option you pick.

         threshold=Dropdown(options=[10, 25, 50, 100], value=25, description="inflation above (percent)", style=WIDE),
         groups=SelectMultiple(options=GROUPS, value=["World"], rows=5, description="groups"));

def all_groups(threshold):
    """Website: Fig. 2 with every group as a line."""
    return high_inflation_share(threshold, GROUPS)

Chart: inspired by Fig. 8.2 in Jones (2024), Macroeconomics, 6th ed.

On the website, click a group in the legend to add it.

What to notice.

  • With the textbook’s threshold of 25 percent, the share was small in the 1960s, jumped in 1974, stayed high in the 1980s and peaked in 1994, when almost one country in three had high inflation.
  • After the mid-1990s the share collapsed. The Covid-19 years brought a small rise, and by 2025 it was down to 3 percent.
  • Choose 10 percent: in 1974, most countries had double-digit inflation. Choose 100 percent: inflation of that size never hit more than about one country in nine, and it peaked in the early 1990s.
  • Add the regions: high inflation came in waves. In Latin America & Caribbean the share reached 41 percent in 1974 and 39 percent in 1991; in Europe & Central Asia it peaked at 40.5 percent in 1993, the years after the Soviet Union broke up; in Sub-Saharan Africa it jumped to 55.6 percent in 1994, when the CFA franc of West and Central Africa was devalued by half. Hover over a line to see how many economies are behind each share: North America and South Asia have only a handful, so their shares jump in big steps.

Key numbers: high inflation over time

The textbook’s description holds: below 6 percent in the 1960s, 31.1 percent in 1994 (“almost one out of every three countries”), and below 5 percent in every year from 2002 to 2021. # Your turn: try it here

Testing the quantity theory

The quantity theory predicts that faster money growth goes with higher inflation. We check it twice, with U.S. decades and with a cross-section of economies.

Fig. 3: Money growth and inflation in the United States

Goal. Test the main prediction of the quantity theory with U.S. history: periods of fast money growth should be periods of high inflation.

Each point is one decade. Money is M2 (currency, checking accounts, savings deposits and money market accounts; see Table 8.2 below). Both growth rates are average annual rates from the first year of a decade to the first year of the next:

\[g = \left(\frac{X_{d+10}}{X_d}\right)^{1/10} - 1\]

decades = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "fig8-3.csv")
decades.tail()
year decade end_year money_growth inflation
11 1980 1980s 1990 7.660 4.724
12 1990 1990s 2000 4.049 2.796
13 2000 2000s 2010 6.078 2.389
14 2010 2010s 2020 7.425 1.728
15 2020 2020s (2020-25) 2025 4.414 4.462

The last row covers only 2020–2025, a decade that is not over yet. To choose other period lengths, and other countries, we load yearly data on money and prices. The Jordà–Schularick–Taylor Macrohistory Database has broad money and the CPI for 18 rich economies since 1870. For the United States the file splices it with M2 from the Federal Reserve after 1958, exactly the series behind fig8-3.csv.

money_panel = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "money_prices_panel.csv")
money_panel.groupby("country").year.agg(["min", "max", "count"]).T
country Australia Belgium Canada Denmark Finland France Germany Ireland Italy Japan Netherlands Norway Portugal Spain Sweden Switzerland United Kingdom United States
min 1870 1979 1871 1870 1870 1870 1870 1922 1870 1870 1870 1870 1870 1874 1871 1880 1870 1870
max 2020 2020 2020 2020 2020 2020 2020 2020 2020 2020 2020 2020 2020 2020 2020 2020 2020 2025
count 151 42 150 151 151 145 140 99 151 151 148 151 151 142 150 141 151 156

money and cpi are indexes in each country’s own units, so only their growth rates can be compared across countries. Two things to notice: the other countries stop in 2020, and some have gaps. Germany has no money data for 1923–1924 (the hyperinflation) and 1939–1947 (the war), and Belgium’s money starts in 1979.

Python note. range(1870, last, years) counts 1870, 1870 + years, … up to the year before last: the first year of each period. min(a, b) is the smaller number, so the last period stops at the last year of data. x ** (1 / n) is the n-th root. and is True only when both conditions are.

def growth(x, start, end):
    """Average annual growth of x from start to end, in percent."""
    return 100 * ((x[end] / x[start]) ** (1 / (end - start)) - 1)


def periods(years=10, country="United States"):
    """Fig. 8.3: average money growth and inflation in periods of `years` years since 1870, for one country."""
    data = money_panel[money_panel.country == country].set_index("year")
    last = data.index.max()
    rows = []
    for start in range(1870, last, years):
        end = min(start + years, last)
        if start in data.index and end in data.index:      # skip periods that start or end in a gap
            label = f"{start}s" if (years == 10 and end - start == 10) else f"{start}–{end}"
            if end - start < years:
                label = label + "*"                       # * marks an unfinished period
            rows.append([country, label, start, end, growth(data.money, start, end), growth(data.cpi, start, end)])
    return pd.DataFrame(rows, columns=["country", "period", "start", "end", "money_growth", "inflation"])


check = periods(10)
print(f"Largest difference from fig8-3.csv: {(check.money_growth - decades.money_growth).abs().max():.3f} (money), "
      f"{(check.inflation - decades.inflation).abs().max():.3f} (inflation)")
Largest difference from fig8-3.csv: 0.000 (money), 0.000 (inflation)

The quantity theory says \(\pi = g_M + g_V - g_Y\). If velocity were constant and real GDP did not grow, every point would lie on the 45-degree line \(\pi = g_M\). Real GDP does grow, so points should lie below that line, by about \(g_Y - g_V\). The chart draws both lines; the lower one is shifted down by the average gap in the data.

Germany’s 1920s are a problem for any chart: money grew by more than 1,000 percent a year on average over the decade. The axes widen once (to 70 percent) when a country needs it, and points beyond that are listed in a note instead of squeezing all the others into a corner.

Python note. .between(a, b) is True for values from a to b. table.drop(shown.index) keeps the rows that are not in shown. .corr() is the correlation of two columns: 1 for points on a rising straight line, 0 for no relation.

KEY_DECADES = ["1870s", "1930s", "1940s", "1970s", "1980s", "2010s", "2020–2025*"]
JST_COUNTRIES = sorted(money_panel.country.unique())
MONEY_COLORS = group_colors(JST_COUNTRIES, [JST_COUNTRIES], BOOK_COLORS)   # the website lists all 18 together


def period_table(years, countries):
    """Fig. 8.3: the periods of all chosen countries, split into points on the chart and points beyond 70%."""
    tables = []
    for country in countries:
        tables.append(periods(years, country))
    table = pd.concat(tables, ignore_index=True)
    inside = table.money_growth.between(-10, 70) & table.inflation.between(-10, 70)
    us_key = (table.country == "United States") & (table.period.isin(KEY_DECADES) | (years == 20))
    table["label"] = table.period.where(us_key, "")   # labels for the textbook's decades; hover shows the rest
    return table[inside], table[~inside]
def add_reference_lines(fig, xr, gap, off):
    """Fig. 8.3: the 45-degree line, the quantity-theory line pi = g_M - gap, and a note on points off the chart."""
    g_M = np.array(xr)
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=g_M, y=g_M, mode="lines", name="π = g_M (45-degree line)", line=dict(color=GRAY, dash="dot")))
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=g_M, y=qt_inflation(g_M, gap), mode="lines", name=f"π = g_M − {gap:.1f}",
                             line=dict(color=GREEN, width=3, dash="dash")))
    fig.add_hline(y=0, line_dash="dash", line_color=GRAY, line_width=1)
    notes = []
    for row in off.itertuples():
        notes.append(f"{row.country} {row.period}: money {row.money_growth:,.0f}%, inflation {row.inflation:,.0f}%")
    if len(notes) > 0:
        fig.add_annotation(x=0.01, y=0.98, xref="paper", yref="paper", xanchor="left", yanchor="top", align="left",
                           showarrow=False, text="Off the chart:<br>" + "<br>".join(notes), font=dict(size=12))
def money_and_prices(years=10, countries=("United States",)):
    """Fig. 8.3: money growth against inflation, one point per period of `years` years and country."""
    shown, off = period_table(years, countries if len(countries) > 0 else ("United States",))
    gap = (shown.money_growth - shown.inflation).mean()
    r = shown.money_growth.corr(shown.inflation)
    fig = px.scatter(shown, x="money_growth", y="inflation", color="country", text="label", hover_name="period",
                     hover_data=["country"], color_discrete_map=MONEY_COLORS,
                     labels={"money_growth": "Money growth (percent per year)", "inflation": "Inflation rate (percent per year)"},
                     title=f"{years}-year periods: correlation {r:.2f}, average gap g_M − π = {gap:.1f} points")
    fig.update_traces(marker=dict(size=11), textposition="top center", textfont=dict(size=11))
    wide = shown.money_growth.max() > 18 or shown.inflation.max() > 17 or shown.inflation.min() < -5
    xr, yr = ([-8, 70], [-10, 70]) if wide else ([-3, 18], [-5, 17])   # widen once, when a country needs it
    if wide:
        fig.update_traces(mode="markers")             # zoomed out, the decade labels would pile up: hover instead
    add_reference_lines(fig, xr, gap, off)
    fig.update_xaxes(range=xr)
    fig.update_yaxes(range=yr)
    fig.update_layout(legend=dict(orientation="h", y=-0.15, yanchor="top"), legend_title_text="")
    return fig
interact(money_and_prices,
         years=Dropdown(options=[5, 10, 20], value=10, description="years per period", style=WIDE),
         countries=SelectMultiple(options=JST_COUNTRIES, value=["United States"], rows=6, description="countries"));

def money_website(years):

    fig = money_and_prices(years)
    tables = []
    for country in JST_COUNTRIES:

                       hover_data=["country"], color_discrete_map=MONEY_COLORS)

        fig.add_trace(t.update(marker_size=9))

Sources. Data: Jordà–Schularick–Taylor Macrohistory Database, release 6, broad money (money) and the CPI (cpi) (Jordà, Schularick and Taylor 2017), 18 economies, 1870–2020; for the United States since 1959, Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System, M2 (M2NS), via FRED, and MeasuringWorth, Officer and Williamson, The Annual Consumer Price Index for the United States, 1774–Present. Prepared files: data/ch08/fig8-3.csv and data/ch08/money_prices_panel.csv (see the data notes). Chart: inspired by Fig. 8.3 in Jones (2024), Macroeconomics, 6th ed.

On the website, click a country in the legend to add its periods; the numbers in the title are for the United States. Germany’s 1920s lie far outside the chart: double-click the plot to zoom back out after adding Germany.

What to notice.

  • With decades, as in the textbook, the 1910s and the 1970s have the fastest inflation and fast money growth. The 1920s and 1930s had slow money growth and deflation: prices fell.
  • The points rise from left to right, roughly parallel to the 45-degree line, and about 4 points below it. The quantity theory says this gap is the growth of real GDP minus the growth of velocity.
  • With 5-year periods the cloud is wider. Wars and the Great Depression move prices a lot over a few years, and the theory is about the long run. Hover over the points to see the periods.
  • With 20-year periods there are only 8 points, all with money growth between 5 and 9 percent.
  • Add Japan, Italy and France. Their 1940s, the war years, sit far up and to the right (Japan: money growth 45 percent and inflation 65 percent a year), and the axes widen to show them: they lie on the same band as everything else. Add Germany: its 1920s are listed in the note, because money grew 1,139 percent a year and prices 1,210 percent. Select all 18 countries: the correlation of the 10-year points is 0.86, and the average gap is 4.0 points, the same as in the United States alone.

Table 8.2: measures of the money supply

What counts as money? The narrowest measure is currency. The monetary base adds the reserves banks hold at the central bank, M1 adds checking accounts, and M2 adds savings and money market accounts. A monthly file from the Federal Reserve has all four, in billions of dollars.

Python note. parse_dates=["date"] turns text such as "2023-01-01" into real dates. .loc[[...]] picks rows by their labels, and .T transposes the table: rows become columns. {last:%B %Y} prints a date as “August 2026”.

supply = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "money_supply.csv", parse_dates=["date"]).set_index("date")
last = supply.index[-1]

January 2023 reproduces the textbook’s table within its rounding. Something odd stands out: M1 is almost as large as M2. Look at the spring of 2020:

supply.loc["2020-03":"2020-07"]
currency monetary_base m1 m2
date
2020-03-01 1838.0 3883.1 4322.9 16034.4
2020-04-01 1891.3 4844.9 4856.4 17064.0
2020-05-01 1931.8 5149.4 16312.5 17931.9
2020-06-01 1958.3 5001.8 16598.6 18180.0
2020-07-01 1981.7 4700.3 16801.3 18331.4

M1 more than triples between April and May 2020, from 4,856 to 16,313 billion dollars. Nobody printed 11 trillion dollars that month: in May 2020 the Federal Reserve changed the definition of M1 and moved savings deposits into it. A jump like this is a series break. Growth rates across the break are meaningless, which is one reason Fig. 3 uses M2, whose definition did not change.

Key numbers: is velocity constant?

The quantity theory assumes a constant velocity. The quantity equation (8.1) lets us measure it: \(V = PY/M\), nominal GDP divided by money. A small annual file has nominal GDP, currency and M2.

yearly = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "us_money_annual.csv").set_index("year")
yearly["velocity"] = yearly.nominal_gdp / yearly.m2
fig = px.line(yearly.reset_index(), x="year", y="velocity", hover_name="year",
              labels={"year": "Year", "velocity": "Velocity of M2 (nominal GDP / M2)"},
              title="M2 velocity stayed near 1.8 until about 1990, then rose and fell")
fig.update_traces(line=dict(color=BLUE, width=3))
fig.update_yaxes(range=[0, 2.5], tickvals=[0.5, 1, 1.5, 2, 2.5])   # no label in the bottom-left corner
fig.show()
print(yearly.velocity.loc[[1960, 1970, 1980, 1990, 1997, 2007, 2021, 2025]].round(2).to_dict())
{1960: 1.78, 1970: 1.78, 1980: 1.86, 1990: 1.85, 1997: 2.18, 2007: 1.98, 2021: 1.16, 2025: 1.41}

Sources. Data: U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis, Gross Domestic Product (GDPA), via FRED; Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System, M2 (M2SL), via FRED, calendar-year averages. Prepared file: data/ch08/us_money_annual.csv (see the data notes). Chart: inspired by the discussion of velocity in Chapter 8 of Jones (2024), Macroeconomics, 6th ed., which has no figure of it.

From 1960 to 1990, M2 velocity stayed between about 1.7 and 1.9, close to the textbook’s assumption. Then it rose to 2.18 in 1997 and fell to 1.16 in 2021, when savings piled up during the pandemic. When velocity falls, money can grow faster than nominal GDP without extra inflation: in equation (8.3) \(\bar{g}_V\) is negative.

Venezuela’s average inflation of 2,614 percent is not an error: it is the hyperinflation of 2017–2021 (Fig. 7), which is not in the textbook’s data. Unlike Venezuela’s GDP numbers in earlier chapters, these numbers are real, so we keep Venezuela and label it.

Inflation ranges from under 1 to over 2,000 percent, so both axes use a ratio scale, as in the textbook. We label a few economies; hover over any point to see its name and how many years of data are behind its two averages.

Python note. .map(LABELS) replaces each code with its label from the dictionary LABELS; codes that are not in it become empty (NaN), and .fillna("") turns those into empty text. np.geomspace(a, b, 200) gives 200 numbers from a to b that are evenly spaced on a ratio scale.

LABELS = {"JPN": "Japan", "CHE": "Switzerland", "DNK": "Denmark", "TUR": "Turkey", "ARG": "Argentina",
          "RUS": "Russia", "GEO": "Georgia", "BRA": "Brazil", "AGO": "Angola", "COD": "Congo, Dem. Rep.",
          "VEN": "Venezuela", "UKR": "Ukraine"}
world["label"] = world.iso3.map(LABELS).fillna("")
POSITIONS = {"COD": "middle left", "BRA": "bottom right", "AGO": "top left"}   # labels that would be cut off or overlap
world["position"] = world.iso3.map(POSITIONS).fillna("middle right")
MONEY_TICKS = [2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 128, 256, 512]
INFLATION_TICKS = [1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 128, 256, 512, 1024, 2048]   # no label in the bottom-left corner
def world_money(g_Y=3.0, period="1990–2025"):
    """Fig. 8.4: average money growth and inflation by economy, with the line pi = g_M - g_Y."""
    suffix = period.replace("–", "_")
    x, y, n_m, n_p = "money_growth_" + suffix, "inflation_" + suffix, "n_money_" + suffix, "n_infl_" + suffix
    above = (world[y] > qt_inflation(world[x], g_Y)).sum()
    fig = px.scatter(world, x=x, y=y, text="label", hover_name="country", log_x=True, log_y=True,
                     hover_data=[n_m, n_p],                       # years behind each average, shown on hover
                     labels={x: f"Money growth, {period} average (percent, ratio scale)",
                             y: "Inflation rate (percent, ratio scale)",
                             n_m: "years of money data", n_p: "years of inflation data"},
                     title=f"π = g_M − g_Y with g_Y = {g_Y:.0f}%: {above} of {len(world)} economies lie above the line")
    fig.update_traces(marker=dict(color=TEAL, size=8), textposition=list(world.position), textfont=dict(color=BLUE, size=11))
    g_M = np.geomspace(g_Y + 0.4, 900, 200)
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=g_M, y=qt_inflation(g_M, g_Y), mode="lines", name=f"Quantity theory, π = g_M − {g_Y:.0f}",
                             line=dict(color=GREEN, width=3, dash="dash")))
    fig.update_xaxes(tickvals=MONEY_TICKS, range=[np.log10(1.5), np.log10(900)])
    fig.update_yaxes(tickvals=INFLATION_TICKS, range=[np.log10(0.3), np.log10(4000)])
    fig.update_layout(legend=dict(x=0.99, y=0.02, xanchor="right", yanchor="bottom"))
    return fig

Sources. Data: World Bank, World Development Indicators, Broad money growth (FM.LBL.BMNY.ZG); World Bank, World Development Indicators, Inflation, consumer prices (FP.CPI.TOTL.ZG), with gaps filled from the World Bank’s Global Inflation Database (Ha, Kose and Ohnsorge 2023). Prepared file: data/ch08/fig8-4.csv (see the data notes). Chart: inspired by Fig. 8.4 in Jones (2024), Macroeconomics, 6th ed.

What to notice.

  • The economies line up along a rising band: the faster money grows, the higher inflation. Brazil, Angola and the Democratic Republic of the Congo have both money growth and inflation in the hundreds of percent.
  • Most economies sit in the dense cloud at the lower left, with money growth of about 10–20 percent and inflation of about 3–18 percent (the middle half of each column, printed below). Japan and Switzerland are near the bottom.
  • With \(g_Y = 0\) the line is the 45-degree line: most economies lie below it, because real GDP grows. On a ratio scale, subtracting \(g_Y\) bends the line down a lot at low money growth and hardly at all at high money growth.
  • Georgia and Venezuela lie far above the band, for a statistical reason. Look at the n_ columns above: their money averages cover fewer years than their inflation averages. In the World Bank data, Georgia’s money series starts in 1996, after its hyperinflation, and Venezuela’s stops in 2013, before its hyperinflation. An average of inflation over crisis years compared with an average of money growth over calm years is not a fair test.

Key numbers: how well does the quantity theory fit?

Python note. np.log10 takes logarithms, the numbers behind a ratio scale. The correlation of the logs measures how close the points are to a straight line on the chart.

for period in ["1990_2021", "1990_2025"]:
    g, p = world["money_growth_" + period], world["inflation_" + period]
    print(f"{period}: correlation of the logs {np.log10(g).corr(np.log10(p)):.2f}; "
          f"median gap g_M - pi {(g - p).median():.1f} points; inflation above money growth in {(p > g).sum()} economies")
print("Middle half of money growth:", world.money_growth_1990_2025.quantile([0.25, 0.75]).round(1).tolist(),
      " of inflation:", world.inflation_1990_2025.quantile([0.25, 0.75]).round(1).tolist())

The textbook’s examples hold in the 1990–2021 averages: Denmark and Switzerland had inflation of 1.8 and 1.0 percent with money growth of about 4–5 percent, while Turkey and Argentina averaged above 25 percent for both. (The World Bank now spells Turkey “Turkiye”.) The correlation of the logs is 0.85 in both periods, and the median economy has money growth 5.6 to 5.8 points above inflation. With constant velocity this gap would be the growth rate of real GDP; a gap this large suggests that velocity fell in many economies, as it did in the United States after 1997.

Real and nominal interest rates

The Fisher equation subtracts inflation from the interest rate a bank pays to get the real return, which is what matters for saving and borrowing.

Fig. 5: Real and nominal interest rates in the United States

Goal. Use the Fisher equation to turn a nominal interest rate into a real one.

The nominal rate is the return on 3-month U.S. Treasury bills, averaged over each year. The real rate cannot be looked up: we compute it with equation (8.6), \(R = i - \pi\), using the CPI inflation of Fig. 1.

rates = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "fig8-5.csv")
rates.head()
year nominal_tbill_3m inflation_cpi real_rate

2 1962 2.773 1.176 1.597
3 1963 3.159 1.256 1.903

The file already has a real_rate column. Let us check it with our function real_rate from “Model overview”.

R = real_rate(rates.nominal_tbill_3m, rates.inflation_cpi)
print(f"Largest difference from the file's real rate: {(R - rates.real_rate).abs().max():.3f} points")
Largest difference from the file's real rate: 0.001 points

The same calculation works for any country with a short-term interest rate. A wider file has 3-month rates for 50 economies (the OECD members and several large emerging economies), with each country’s CPI inflation from the panel of Fig. 1:

rates_panel = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "interest_rates_panel.csv")
rates_panel[rates_panel.year == 2024].head()
iso3 country year short_rate inflation real_rate rate_source
25 ARG Argentina 2024 55.656 219.884 -164.228 OECD EO
83 AUS Australia 2024 4.391 3.167 1.224 OECD EO
142 AUT Austria 2024 3.572 2.938 0.634 OECD EO
208 BEL Belgium 2024 3.572 3.144 0.428 OECD EO
238 BRA Brazil 2024 11.088 4.367 6.720 OECD EO

rate_source says where the rate comes from. For the United States it is the Treasury-bill rate of the textbook. For the other countries it is the OECD’s 3-month money-market (interbank) rate, a rate at which banks lend to each other. That is a slightly different rate: in the United States the OECD’s 3-month rate has been 0.6 points above the Treasury-bill rate on average.

Before plotting, we give the columns readable names for the legend. Inflation is hidden at first; click it in the legend to show it. Hover over the chart to read all three numbers of a year and check that \(i = R + \pi\). Rates in some countries were much higher than in the United States, so the vertical axis widens in steps.

RATE_RANGES = [[-10, 16], [-20, 32], [-40, 64], [-80, 128], [-200, 250]]


def rate_range(low, high):
    """The first range in RATE_RANGES that contains both low and high (the widest one if none does)."""
    for bottom, top in RATE_RANGES:
        if bottom <= low and high <= top:
            return [bottom, top]
    return RATE_RANGES[-1]
def interest_rates(country="United States"):
    """Fig. 8.5: the nominal rate i, the real rate R = i - pi and inflation pi of one country."""
    data = rates_panel[rates_panel.country == country]
    named = data.rename(columns={"short_rate": "Nominal rate, i", "real_rate": "Real rate, R = i − π",
                                 "inflation": "Inflation, π"})
    negative = (data.real_rate < 0).sum()
    fig = px.line(named, x="year", y=["Nominal rate, i", "Real rate, R = i − π", "Inflation, π"], hover_name="year",
                  color_discrete_sequence=[BLUE, GREEN, ORANGE], labels={"year": "Year", "value": "Percent"},
                  title=f"{country}: the real rate R = i − π was negative in {negative} of {data.real_rate.count()} years")
    fig.update_traces(line=dict(width=3))
    fig.update_traces(selector=dict(name="Inflation, π"), visible="legendonly", line=dict(dash="dot"))
    fig.add_hline(y=0, line_dash="dash", line_color=GRAY)
    yr = rate_range(data[["short_rate", "inflation", "real_rate"]].min().min(),
                    data[["short_rate", "inflation", "real_rate"]].max().max())
    fig.update_yaxes(range=yr, tickvals=[-5, 0, 5, 10, 15] if yr == [-10, 16] else None)   # no label in the corner
    fig.update_xaxes(range=[1959, 2026])
    fig.update_layout(hovermode="x unified", legend=dict(orientation="h", y=-0.15, yanchor="top"), legend_title_text="")
    return fig
interact(interest_rates, country=Dropdown(options=sorted(rates_panel.country.unique()), value="United States",
                                          description="country", style=WIDE));

On the website, choose a country in the menu at the top left.

What to notice.

  • The nominal rate is high when inflation is high. It peaked at just over 14 percent in 1981, a year after inflation peaked.
  • The real rate was negative in the 1970s, in most years since 2008, and sharply negative in 2021–2022, when inflation jumped while the nominal rate was still near zero.
  • In 2009 the real rate was above the nominal rate. Show inflation in the legend: it was negative that year.
  • Choose Germany. In 1974 the U.S. real rate was −3.2 percent, but Germany’s was +2.9 percent: its central bank fought the inflation of the 1970s earlier and harder, and German inflation never went above 7 percent (Fig. 1).
  • Choose Turkey: in 2022 its short rate was 14 percent and inflation 72 percent, a real rate of −58 percent by \(R = i - \pi\). With rates this high the shortcut is poor; the exact real rate, \((1+i)/(1+\pi) - 1\), is −34 percent.

Key numbers: real rates

r = rates.set_index("year")
print(f"Highest nominal rate: {r.nominal_tbill_3m.max():.1f}% in {r.nominal_tbill_3m.idxmax()}")
print(f"2009: nominal {r.nominal_tbill_3m[2009]:.2f}%, inflation {r.inflation_cpi[2009]:.2f}%, real {r.real_rate[2009]:.2f}%")
print("Years with a negative real rate:", r.index[r.real_rate < 0].tolist())
print(f"Lowest real rate: {r.real_rate.min():.2f}% in {r.real_rate.idxmin()};  {r.index[-1]}: {r.real_rate.iloc[-1]:.2f}%")
print(f"Average real rate: 1960-2022 {r.real_rate.loc[:2022].mean():.2f}%, 1960-2007 {r.real_rate.loc[:2007].mean():.2f}%")

2009: nominal 0.15%, inflation -0.32%, real 0.47%
Years with a negative real rate: [1974, 1975, 1976, 1977, 1978, 1979, 1980, 2003, 2004, 2005, 2008, 2010, 2011, 2012, 2013, 2014, 2015, 2016, 2017, 2018, 2020, 2021, 2022]
Lowest real rate: -5.97% in 2022;  2025: 1.43%

Most of the textbook’s statements hold: a nominal peak of 14.0 percent in 1981, a real rate above the nominal rate in 2009, negative real rates in 2003 and in every year from 2010 to 2018, and −5.97 percent in 2022. One does not: the textbook says the real rate averages “about 1.5 percent” over the period, but the plotted series averages 0.59 percent over 1960–2022 (1.31 percent over 1960–2007). Since 2023 the real rate has been positive again.

Hyperinflation and high inflation

Finally, the extreme cases: inflation of hundreds or thousands of percent a year, why it starts and how it can end.

Fig. 6: Hyperinflations in Argentina, Brazil, and Russia

Goal. See how extreme inflation can get, and how quickly a hyperinflation can end.

A hyperinflation is inflation above about 500 percent a year. The textbook’s file has annual CPI inflation for three countries that went through one, and the file of Fig. 8.7 three more. We load both now, because Figs. 6 and 7 share one table.

hyper = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "fig8-6.csv")
hyper = hyper.rename(columns={"argentina": "Argentina", "brazil": "Brazil", "russia": "Russia"})
latam = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "fig8-7.csv")
latam = latam.rename(columns={"mexico": "Mexico", "nigeria": "Nigeria", "venezuela": "Venezuela"})
hyper.head()

Two gaps, compared with the textbook: the World Bank no longer publishes Argentina’s inflation before 1970, so the line starts in 1970; and Argentina before 2018 comes from the Global Inflation Database, because the WDI has dropped those years. Brazil starts in 1981 and Russia in 1993.

Data hygiene: Zimbabwe

Every other country comes from the panel of Fig. 1. Before using it, look at one country the textbook mentions, Zimbabwe, whose hyperinflation peaked in November 2008:

panel[(panel.country == "Zimbabwe") & (panel.year >= 2000) & (panel.year <= 2009)]
iso3 country year inflation source
10817 ZWE Zimbabwe 2000 4.475 GID
10818 ZWE Zimbabwe 2001 -37.198 GID
10819 ZWE Zimbabwe 2002 -34.445 GID
10820 ZWE Zimbabwe 2003 -8.565 GID
10821 ZWE Zimbabwe 2004 113.569 GID
10822 ZWE Zimbabwe 2005 -31.522 GID
10823 ZWE Zimbabwe 2006 32.974 GID
10824 ZWE Zimbabwe 2007 -72.729 GID
10825 ZWE Zimbabwe 2008 156.964 GID
10826 ZWE Zimbabwe 2009 6.216 GID

These numbers cannot be right. They say that prices fell by 73 percent in 2007 and rose only 157 percent in 2008, when, according to the textbook, prices were doubling roughly every day. Zimbabwe’s official price statistics broke down during the crisis, and no reliable annual series exists. We drop Zimbabwe’s values for 2001–2008. (The same years enter Zimbabwe’s average in Fig. 4, so its point there is not reliable either.)

Python note. ~ means “not”: panel[~bad] keeps every row where bad is False. .melt(id_vars="year", ...) turns the country columns of the textbook’s files into rows, one row per country and year, the shape of the panel. HIGH lists Fig. 7’s countries (peaks of 100 to 500 percent, | adds the textbook’s three), and PATH_COLORS gives the countries of each list different colors.

bad = (panel.country == "Zimbabwe") & (panel.year >= 2001) & (panel.year <= 2008)
clean = panel[~bad]
book = pd.concat([hyper.melt(id_vars="year", var_name="country", value_name="inflation"),
                  latam.melt(id_vars="year", var_name="country", value_name="inflation")]).dropna()
paths = pd.concat([book, clean[~clean.country.isin(book.country.unique())]], ignore_index=True)   # textbook files, then the panel
peaks = paths.groupby("country").inflation.max()
HYPER = sorted(peaks[peaks > 500].index)
HIGH = sorted(set(peaks[(peaks > 100) & (peaks <= 500)].index) | {"Mexico", "Nigeria", "Venezuela"})   # Fig. 7's list
PATH_COLORS = group_colors(sorted(paths.country.unique()), [HYPER, HIGH], BOOK_COLORS)
print(len(HYPER), "economies with at least one year above 500%:", HYPER)
31 economies with at least one year above 500%: ['Angola', 'Argentina', 'Armenia', 'Azerbaijan', 'Belarus', 'Bolivia', 'Brazil', 'Bulgaria', 'Chile', 'Congo, Dem. Rep.', 'Croatia', 'Estonia', 'Georgia', 'Indonesia', 'Kazakhstan', 'Kyrgyz Republic', 'Latvia', 'Lithuania', 'Moldova', 'Nicaragua', 'North Macedonia', 'Peru', 'Poland', 'Russia', 'Slovenia', 'Tajikistan', 'Turkmenistan', 'Ukraine', 'Uzbekistan', 'Venezuela', 'Zimbabwe']

On a linear scale, the peaks of thousands of percent flatten everything else. A ratio scale shows every level of inflation at once, but it cannot show zero or negative rates: Argentina’s deflation of 2001 (−1.1 percent) simply leaves a gap. The axes widen when a country with a higher peak is added.

RATIO_TICKS = [0.3, 1, 3, 10, 30, 100, 300, 1000, 3000, 10000, 30000, 100000]   # no label in the bottom-left corner
LINEAR_TICKS = [500, 1000, 1500, 2000, 2500, 3000]                            # (the textbook's linear scale)
LINEAR_TOPS = [3500, 7000, 15000, 75000]


def disinflation(data):
    """Figs. 8.6-8.7: the highest peak among the chosen countries, and when that country fell below 25%."""
    top = data.loc[data.inflation.idxmax()]
    own = data[data.country == top.country]
    later = own[(own.year > top.year) & (own.inflation < 25)]
    if len(later) > 0:
        return f"{top.country}: {top.inflation:,.0f}% in {top.year:.0f}, below 25% by {later.year.min():.0f}"
    return f"{top.country}: {top.inflation:,.0f}% in {top.year:.0f}, still above 25% in {own.year.max():.0f}"
def inflation_paths(countries=("Argentina", "Brazil", "Russia"), scale="linear"):
    """Figs. 8.6 and 8.7: inflation in the chosen countries, on a linear or a ratio scale."""
    data = paths[paths.country.isin(countries if len(countries) > 0 else ("Argentina",))]
    title = disinflation(data)
    if scale == "ratio":
        data = data[data.inflation > 0]                  # a ratio scale cannot show zero or falling prices
    fig = px.line(data, x="year", y="inflation", color="country", log_y=(scale == "ratio"), hover_name="country",
                  color_discrete_map=PATH_COLORS, title=title,
                  labels={"year": "Year", "inflation": "Inflation rate (percent)", "country": "Country"})
    fig.update_traces(line=dict(width=3))
    fig.add_hline(y=500, line_dash="dot", line_color=GRAY, annotation_text="500%: hyperinflation",
                  annotation_position="bottom left")
    peak = data.inflation.max()
    if scale == "ratio":
        top = 5000 if peak < 5000 else 200000
        fig.update_yaxes(tickvals=RATIO_TICKS, range=[np.log10(0.1), np.log10(top)])
    else:
        top = axis_top(1.1 * peak, LINEAR_TOPS)
        fig.update_yaxes(tickvals=LINEAR_TICKS if top == 3500 else None, range=[-top / 35, top])
    fig.update_xaxes(range=[1960, 2026])
    fig.update_layout(hovermode="x unified", legend_title_text="")
    return fig

Python note. Several widgets in one interact call: each argument of the function gets its own widget.

fig.update_layout(title=inflation_paths(("Argentina", "Brazil", "Russia"), "linear").layout.title)   # the title of the default view
legend_only(fig, ["Argentina", "Brazil", "Russia"])

Prepared files: data/ch08/fig8-6.csv, data/ch08/fig8-7.csv and data/ch08/inflation_panel.csv (see the data notes). Chart: inspired by Fig. 8.6 in Jones (2024), Macroeconomics, 6th ed.

On the website, click a country in the legend to add it; the axis adapts.

What to notice.

  • Argentina had high inflation for decades, with spikes in 1976 and 1984–1985 before the peak of 1989. Brazil peaked in 1990 and again in 1993–1994; Russia’s series starts at 874 percent in 1993.
  • Each hyperinflation ended within a few years: Argentina was below 5 percent by 1994, Brazil by 1998.
  • Switch to the ratio scale. It shows what the linear scale hides: Argentina’s inflation climbed again in the 2010s and 2020s, to 220 percent in 2024, while Brazil’s and Russia’s stayed low.
  • Add Ukraine, another former Soviet republic: 4,735 percent in 1993, and below 25 percent by 1997, the same pattern as Russia. The title always reports the highest peak among the countries you show.

The inflation tax

Why would a government let money grow so fast? Because printing money is one way to pay its bills. The government budget constraint says that spending \(G\) is paid with taxes \(T\), new borrowing \(\Delta B\), or new money \(\Delta M\):

\[G = T + \Delta B + \Delta M \qquad (8.7)\]

The revenue from new money is called seignorage, or the inflation tax. It is paid by everyone who holds money: when the price level doubles, a 200-dollar bill buys only what 100 dollars bought before.

def money_printed(G, T, dB):
    """Equation (8.7): the new money the government must issue, Delta M = G - T - Delta B."""
    return G - T - dB


print(f"Spending 25% of GDP, taxes 20%, new borrowing 2%: new money = {money_printed(25, 20, 2):.0f}% of GDP")
print(f"If lenders stop lending (new borrowing 0%):        new money = {money_printed(25, 20, 0):.0f}% of GDP")
print(f"Real value of 200 dollars of currency after prices double: {200 / 2:.0f} dollars of today")
Spending 25% of GDP, taxes 20%, new borrowing 2%: new money = 3% of GDP
If lenders stop lending (new borrowing 0%):        new money = 5% of GDP
Real value of 200 dollars of currency after prices double: 100 dollars of today

In the United States, the inflation tax is tiny. Measured as new currency issued each year, as a percentage of GDP:

Python note. .diff() gives the change from the previous row: here, the currency added in each year.

yearly["new_currency"] = 100 * yearly.currency.diff() / yearly.nominal_gdp
print(yearly.new_currency.loc[[1975, 1980, 2000, 2020, 2025]].round(2).to_dict())
print(f"Largest: {yearly.new_currency.max():.2f}% of GDP in {yearly.new_currency.idxmax()}")
{1975: 0.4, 1980: 0.38, 2000: 0.34, 2020: 0.96, 2025: 0.15}
Largest: 0.96% of GDP in 2020

Even in the Great Inflation, new currency brought in about 0.4 percent of GDP, and the largest value since 1960 is under 1 percent of GDP, in 2020. The textbook reports that countries with high inflation typically raise about 5 percent of GDP or less this way, and Argentina more than 10 percent in the late 1970s and early 1980s. That is why Thomas Sargent calls persistent high inflation “a fiscal phenomenon”.

Your turn. A government spends 30 percent of GDP and collects 22 percent in taxes. How much must it borrow to issue no new money at all? Check your answer with money_printed.

Hint

Set \(\Delta M = 0\) in equation (8.7) and solve for \(\Delta B\). Then money_printed(30, 22, ...) should give 0.

Prepared files: data/ch08/fig8-7.csv, data/ch08/fig8-6.csv and data/ch08/inflation_panel.csv (see the data notes). Chart: inspired by Fig. 8.7 in Jones (2024), Macroeconomics, 6th ed.

On the website, click a country in the legend to add it. The list holds the countries whose inflation peaked between 100 and 500 percent: high inflation that never became a hyperinflation.

What to notice.

  • Mexico (peaks of 102 percent in 1983 and 132 percent in 1987) and Nigeria (73 percent in 1995) had high inflation, but never a hyperinflation by the 500-percent definition. Both came down within a few years.
  • Venezuela crossed 500 percent in 2018 and stayed above it until 2021. By 2024 inflation was down to 49 percent.
  • Add Bolivia, Nicaragua or Peru: the Latin American hyperinflations of the 1980s and early 1990s reached thousands of percent. Bolivia’s fell from its 1985 peak to 15 percent by 1987; Nicaragua’s and Peru’s took four or five years.
  • Add Turkey: inflation above 25 percent in most years from the late 1970s to 2003, with a peak of 105 percent in 1994, but never a hyperinflation. High inflation can last for decades without exploding.

Key numbers: Venezuela and the definition of hyperinflation

Concluding remarks

  • Inflation is the growth rate of the price level. U.S. inflation peaked at 13.5 percent in 1980, stayed near 2 percent for two decades, and jumped to 8 percent in 2022. A price index turns past prices into today’s dollars.
  • The quantity theory of money gives \(P^* = \bar{M}\bar{V}/\bar{Y}\) and \(\pi^* = \bar{g}_M - \bar{g}_Y\): in the long run, faster money growth means higher inflation, one for one. U.S. decades and 165 economies line up as predicted, although velocity is not really constant.
  • The Fisher equation \(i = R + \pi\) turns nominal interest rates into real ones. U.S. real rates were negative in the 1970s and in most years since 2008.
  • Hyperinflations happen when governments cannot pay their bills with taxes or borrowing and print money instead: persistent high inflation is a fiscal problem. They can end as quickly as they start.
  • The next chapter starts the short-run part of the book, with an introduction to economic fluctuations.
